lessons.title: Dairy systems and herd planning
lessons.html:
Dairy systems in South Africa

South African dairies fall broadly into two types. Pasture-based systems, common in the Eastern Cape, Western Cape coast and KwaZulu-Natal midlands, rely on irrigated or rain-fed ryegrass and kikuyu with concentrate supplements, often using Jersey or crossbred cows. Total mixed ration (TMR) systems, common inland, house Holsteins and feed a mixed ration of silage, hay and concentrates. Each has different costs, labour needs and risks; the manager must choose the system that fits the farm's climate, water and capital.

Herd structure and calving pattern

Profit depends on cows calving regularly. Targets commonly used are a calving interval close to 12 to 13 months and a planned replacement rate. A seasonal calving herd concentrates calving so that peak lactation matches peak pasture growth; a year-round herd evens out milk supply for the buyer. Plan heifer rearing so replacements calve at the target age and weight.

The lactation cycle

  1. Early lactation: milk rises to a peak; intake lags behind, so cows lose condition. Feed well and watch for metabolic disease.
  2. Mid lactation: breed back; milk slowly declines.
  3. Late lactation: rebuild condition.
  4. Dry period: usually about six to eight weeks before calving, allowing udder repair. Transition management in the three weeks before and after calving is critical.

Key performance indicators

KPIWhy it matters
Litres per cow per day and per hectareProduction efficiency
Butterfat and protein %Milk price
Somatic cell countUdder health, price penalties
Calving interval, conception rateFertility
Feed cost per litreMargin over feed

lessons.title: Milking management and milk quality
lessons.html:
Producing safe, high-quality milk

Milk is food. Producers must meet hygiene and quality standards set by regulations and by the milk buyer, who tests every collection. Penalties for high bacterial counts, high cell counts or residues cut income quickly.

Milking routine

  1. Bring cows in calmly; stress releases adrenaline and blocks milk let-down.
  2. Fore-strip a few squirts from each quarter into a strip cup to detect clinical mastitis.
  3. Pre-dip or wash, then dry teats with individual paper or cloth towels.
  4. Attach units within about a minute of preparation for good let-down.
  5. Avoid over-milking; check that automatic cluster removers work.
  6. Post-dip teats with an approved teat dip.

Mastitis control

Mastitis is the costliest dairy disease. Control rests on hygiene, a well-maintained milking machine (serviced regularly and checked for vacuum level and pulsation), dry cow therapy as prescribed by your vet, culling chronic cases and clean, dry housing or paddocks.

Residues and the bulk tank

Mark treated cows clearly (leg bands or spray) and milk them last into a separate bucket. Keep their milk out of the bulk tank for the full withholding period on the label or prescription. Even a small amount of antibiotic milk can contaminate a whole tanker load, and the farm can be held liable.

Cooling and cleaning

Cool milk quickly after milking and keep it cold until collection. Clean the plant after every milking using the correct hot water temperatures and detergents supplied for the system. Record tank temperatures and cleaning routines.

Safety in the parlour

Cows can kick and crush. Stay out of kicking range, use correct parlour design, keep floors non-slip and wear gloves and eye protection when handling acid and alkaline cleaning chemicals.

lessons.title: Feeding, health and financial management
lessons.html:
Running the dairy as a business

Feeding

Feed is usually the biggest cost. Formulate rations with a nutritionist to match stage of lactation, and keep enough effective fibre to prevent acidosis. Monitor body condition, dung consistency, milk butterfat (a drop can indicate rumen problems) and feed refusals daily. On pasture systems, measure grass cover and allocate fresh strips to manage intake.

Health programme

Work with your vet on vaccination, transition cow care (milk fever, ketosis, retained afterbirth), lameness control through hoof trimming and footbaths, calf rearing (colostrum within the first hours of life is essential) and testing for brucellosis and tuberculosis as required. Record every treatment.

Financial management

Track margin over feed cost per cow per day: milk income minus feed cost. Watch it monthly alongside milk price. Other major costs are labour, electricity, repairs, replacements, vet and interest. Calculate cost per litre and compare it with the milk price; if cost per litre is rising faster than price, find out why.

Example: a 300-cow herd producing 22 litres per cow per day at a milk price of R7,00 per litre earns about R46 200 per day. If feed costs R4,00 per litre, margin over feed is about R19 800 per day before other costs.

People

Dairies run every day of the year. Good rosters, training, fair labour practices and a safe workplace under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 reduce staff turnover, which directly affects cow care and milk quality.

Key points

  • Choose the dairy system that suits the farm's climate, water and capital.
  • Fertility and transition cow care drive herd profitability.
  • A consistent milking routine and machine maintenance control mastitis.
  • Keep treated milk out of the tank for the full withholding period.
  • Manage margin over feed cost and cost per litre.
